name: Liam Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a salaried doctor at the surgery on Market Square, in a market town of about twenty thousand people. It's owned by four partners, and I'm the youngest doctor there by about fifteen years. A normal day is thirty-odd appointments, a phone list at lunch, and an afternoon of results: blood tests, scans, letters from the hospital. I like that it's never the same twice; what wears me down is the phone list, which can be forty calls long.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said the partners own the surgery. Are you hoping to become one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's the plan, yes, in three or four years if they offer it. It means buying a share in the business, which I can't afford yet, because I'm still paying off a credit card from my exam fees and the move here. I use AI now and then, mostly to check drug interactions or summarise a new guideline, but only the tools the partners have approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out about as I expected: useful in places, oversold overall. At work we'd have a laugh about the sales reps who promised us the moon. I'd probably not post anything; I'm not much of a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the slow plan carries on. Clear the credit card in about a year, start saving for the partnership buy-in, keep my head down. The trouble is that I've got less than a month of money, so a broken boiler or a car repair sets everything back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and use the approved tools for the dull bits. I'd put an extra hundred a month onto the credit card until it's gone. And I'd ask Dr Hughes, the senior partner, whether the partnership offer is still realistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. Not thrilled, not worried, just a bit stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra hundred a month come out of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, mainly, and the second five-a-side league I joined in spring. I'd keep one league, because that's my sanity. Cooking at home isn't a hardship; I'm a decent cook when I bother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Dr Hughes would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that it's still on, but 'when the time is right', which is what he says about everything. The partners are cautious people. In this picture, though, I think the offer would come.

say: AI turned out about as **expected**: useful in places, oversold overall.
He'd **laugh** at work about sales reps who promised the moon, and not post.
think: The **slow plan** carries on: clear the card, then save for the partnership buy-in.
With less than **a month** saved, one boiler or car repair sets everything back.
do: Pay an extra **hundred a month** onto the credit card until it's cleared.
Ask **Dr Hughes** whether the partnership offer is still realistic.
Keep using the **approved tools** for dull tasks like interaction checks.
feel: Fairly **steady**, but stretched by money rather than worried by AI.
S0.quote: AI turned out about as I expected: useful in places, oversold overall.
fieldNote: His career goal is to **buy into the partnership**, which shapes every answer.
A **credit card** from exam fees and moving is his main pressure.
He's **pragmatic** and low-key, more likely to cook at home than complain.

steps.text: Pay an extra hundred a month onto the credit card
Ask Dr Hughes whether the partnership offer still stands

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of this is genuinely good, like getting rid of the phone list, and some needs watching. I'd say that at practice meetings, calmly. I'd want to see what the other surgeries in the area do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my own job is probably safe, because the partners need a doctor in the room. But the partnership looks different. If AI does the letters, results and booking, the surgery needs fewer staff, and the partners might keep the profit rather than bring in a new partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see which tools the other surgeries in the area actually like, then learn those properly. I'd volunteer to take on the results workload with the new software, since I'm the youngest. And I'd keep paying off the card so I'm ready if a buy-in is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly uneasy. It's on my mind on the drive home, not at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for other surgeries rather than go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first surgeries to try new software always find the problems, and I'd rather they found them. I'm not against it, I just like proof. Once two or three practices I trust are using something, I'll pick it up quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the surgery would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin team, five people, mostly women who've worked here for years. Pat runs the reception and knows every patient's family. If the phone list goes to software, I'm not sure the partners would keep all five on.

say: Some of it is **genuinely good**, like ending the forty-call phone list.
He'd want to see what **other surgeries** do first, and say so calmly.
think: His own job is **probably safe**, because the partners need a doctor in the room.
The **partnership** looks less likely if partners keep the AI savings as profit.
do: Wait a few months, then **learn the tools** that nearby surgeries rate.
Volunteer to run the **results workload** on the new software.
Keep paying off the **credit card** to be ready for a buy-in.
feel: Mildly **uneasy**, on his mind on the drive home but not at night.
S1.quote: The first surgeries to try new software always find the problems, and I'd rather they found them.
fieldNote: He's a **classic steady adopter**: waits for proof, then moves quickly.
The threat he sees is to his **partnership prospects**, not his job.
He worries for the **admin team**, five people, more than himself.

steps.text: Wait to learn the tools nearby surgeries rate

Keep paying the credit card down each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and I'd say it at the practice meeting without much sugar on it. With friends I'd say I didn't spend eleven years training to be replaced in two. I'd still try to be calm in public, because patients pick up on panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the partnership dream is dead in this one. By 2028 the thinking part of the job, which is most of a doctor's value, is done better and cheaper by software. The partners might keep one or two doctors for examinations until the robots come around 2031, and I'm the newest, so I'm first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the partnership savings and turn everything into an emergency fund. I'd look for work abroad, somewhere slower to adopt it, maybe through a medical recruiter, because a doctor's licence still travels. I'd cut the five-a-side, the car, anything that isn't rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The plan I've been building for three years just vanishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving abroad is a big step. Would you really do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the alternative is being out of work at twenty-nine, yes. I've got no partner, no kids, no house. If anyone can move, it's me, and I'd rather go than wait to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine and I've got a plan, which would be half true. My parents spent a lot to help me through medical school. I'd hate for them to think it was wasted.

say: We're **not ready**, and he'd say it bluntly at the practice meeting.
He'd stay **calm in public**, because patients pick up on panic.
think: The **partnership dream** is dead, as software does most thinking work by 2028.
As the **newest doctor**, he expects to be first out before robots arrive in 2031.
do: Turn partnership savings into an **emergency fund**.
Contact a **medical recruiter** about work abroad, where adoption is slower.
Cut the **five-a-side**, the car and everything but rent and food.
S2.quote: I didn't spend eleven years training to be replaced in two.
fieldNote: As the **newest** doctor at a partner-owned surgery, he expects to go first.
He'd **move abroad** before waiting to be let go, citing no partner, children or house.
He's protective of his **parents'** sense that his training was worth it.

steps.text: Turn partnership savings into an emergency fund
Contact a medical recruiter about work abroad
Sell the car and drop the five-a-side league

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable if the surgery plans now. At the practice meeting I'd ask for a proper plan for each of us, not just the partners. With friends I'd be honest that it worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years lets me make myself the doctor they keep. I'd learn the AI systems properly, and I'd train in hands-on procedures like skin surgery and joint injections, which last until robots come around 2034. The partnership is probably off, but a job isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the minor surgery course next year, which costs about a month's pay, after clearing the credit card. I'd get properly good at the AI results system, so I'm the one who runs it. And I'd build up three months of savings over the five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but busy. Five years feels like a race I could win if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a month's pay for the course realistic with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. Card first, then six months of saving, then the course. I'd ask the partners to split the cost, since they'd benefit from a doctor who can do skin surgery in-house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd be thirty-five, with a lot of skills that robots can now do. I'd hope by then there's some plan from the government, because one doctor can't plan for that alone.

He'd ask for a **plan for each doctor**, not just the partners.

Become the doctor who runs the **AI results system**.

S3.quote: Five years feels like a race I could win if I start now.
fieldNote: He gives up on the **partnership** but not on the job.

steps.text: Take the minor surgery course after clearing the card
Become the surgery's lead on the AI results system
Build three months of savings over five years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this well, and the surgery should start planning now. At the practice meeting I'd push for a ten-year plan. With friends I'd be fairly relaxed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I might end up as a partner after all, and that could work in my favour. If I buy in around 2030, I'd own part of a business that uses AGI to see more patients with fewer staff. I'd be thirty-seven when thinking work goes, forty when robots come, with a share in what replaces it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the card, save for the buy-in, and ask Dr Hughes for a firm timeline. I'd learn the AI systems as they're proven. I'd also do a short course on running a practice, because owning a business is different from being a doctor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It's the one where I have a seat at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you worry about the admin team. Would owning the surgery change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make it my decision, which is worse in a way. I'd want to retrain them into patient support roles rather than let them go. Whether the other partners would agree, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in profiting from the change you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I'd rather name it. If the surgery uses AI either way, I'd rather be one of the owners making decisions than an employee waiting for them. It's pragmatic, not proud.

say: Ten years is **enough time** to do this well, if planning starts now.
He'd push for a **ten-year plan** at the practice meeting.
think: He might become a **partner** after all, and own part of the change.
At thirty-seven he'd hold a **share** in what replaces the thinking work.
do: Clear the card and save for the **partnership buy-in**.
Ask Dr Hughes for a **firm timeline** on the offer.

feel: Uneasy but **mostly fine**, with a seat at the table.
S4.quote: If the surgery uses AI either way, I'd rather be one of the owners making decisions than an employee waiting for them.
fieldNote: Ten years turns AGI from a threat into a possible **ownership stake**.
He names his own **contradiction** about profiting from change he worries about.
Owning the surgery makes the **admin team's fate** his own decision, which he finds harder.

steps.text: Save for the partnership buy-in around 2030
Ask Dr Hughes for a firm partnership timeline

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be the newest doctor at a surgery that suddenly needs fewer of us, with no savings. What would help is a clear national plan for doctors, so it's not each surgery deciding on its own. And some help with retraining costs, so it doesn't come out of a credit card.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe where young doctors fit. Everyone talks about older workers near retirement, but I've got thirty-five years of career ahead of me and debt behind me, and nobody's planning for my age group.

headlineQuote: I've got thirty-five years of career ahead of me and debt behind me, and nobody's planning for my age group.
portrait: Liam is a **27-year-old** salaried doctor at a partner-owned surgery on Market Square in a small market town.
He's paying off a **credit card** from exam fees and moving, with under a month saved.
He uses **approved AI tools** now and then and waits for proof before adopting more.
Fast AGI **kills** his partnership plan; he'd look for work abroad.
With ten years he'd **buy in** and own part of the change, while naming the contradiction.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, as the **newest doctor** at a surgery suddenly needing fewer of them.
whatWouldHelp: A **national plan** for doctors and help with **retraining costs** so they don't go on a credit card.
